title: Restrict Registry Permissions
summary: Restrict Registry Permissions is the hardening of the configuration database that Windows and its applications rely on, so that only authorised identities can change the settings that decide how the system behaves. The mechanism matters because the registry is not passive storage. Values in it define which programs start automatically, which services run, which drivers load, how the network resolves names, and which security settings apply, so write access to a key is often equivalent to code execution or persistence. In real environments the work includes reviewing access control entries on sensitive hives such as the machine-wide run and service keys, removing write rights from ordinary users, correcting keys that were loosened to make an old application work, protecting the keys that define authentication and remote access behaviour, and monitoring changes to startup and security related locations. Evidence appears as registry modification events where auditing is enabled, changes to run and service keys, and the appearance of entries that reference unusual paths or command interpreters. The common misunderstandings are that the registry is too complex to review and that a full hive is the right unit of control. Control is per key, and the keys that matter are a small, well documented set. A second misunderstanding is that removal of a value is enough; a key can be recreated by any process that still holds write access to its parent, so the parent permission is the real decision. Because legitimate installers and management agents also write to these keys, baselining normal change is more useful than blocking all change.

beginner.definition: The registry is a settings database inside Windows. It stores options for programs, services, drivers, and security. Restricting registry permissions means only trusted accounts and programs may change the important parts of that database.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many settings in the registry decide what starts when Windows boots. An attacker who can change them can make harmful code run after every restart. That code then survives a simple cleanup. Weak permissions also let someone switch off security features quietly. Because the registry is rarely inspected, changes there can stay hidden for a long time.
howItWorks: Find the registry areas that control startup programs, services, drivers, and security settings.
Check who currently has permission to change each of those areas, including normal user accounts.
Remove write access from anyone who does not need it, and keep the change well documented.
Turn on auditing for those areas so every change is recorded with the account that made it.
Watch the records for entries pointing to unusual folders or command line tools.
Baseline the changes your own installers make, so you can tell routine work from abuse.
beginner.example: Think of a building control room. It holds the switches for the lights, the lifts, and the fire doors. Staff may look through the window at any time. Only a few engineers hold the key to the panel. Every switch they touch is written in a log book. If the panel were left open, a visitor could stop a lift or turn off the alarms. Registry permissions are the lock and the log book for that control room.
takeaways: Write access to the right registry key is almost as powerful as running code.
Removing a harmful entry is pointless if the account can simply create it again.
Record what your own installers change, otherwise every alert becomes noise.

objectives: Explain why registry write access is equivalent to persistence or configuration change.
Identify the registry locations that most affect security and startup behaviour.
Describe how inheritance affects the permissions that actually apply to a key.
Explain how to audit and baseline legitimate registry change.
Plan a review that distinguishes routine installers from suspicious modification.
